10660-lives-of-the-english-poets-from-jo:
Henry Francis Cary, best known as the translator of Dante, wrote Lives of the English Poets from Johnson to Kirke White as a sequel to Samuel Johnson's famous Lives. Published in 1846, the volume carries the story of English poetry from Johnson's age into the early nineteenth century, ending with the short-lived poet Kirke White.

Cary's notices mix biography with criticism, judging each poet's work and place in the tradition. An editor's preface notes that the papers first appeared in a literary journal. Readers get a bridge between Johnson's eighteenth century and the Romantic age, written by a scholar who knew both well.
11221-the-bent-twig:
Dorothy Canfield published this 1915 novel, The Bent Twig, in four books: In Arcadia, A False Start to Athens, In Capua at Last, and The Strait Path. Sylvia Marshall grows up in La Chance, where chapters cover her home, the Marshalls' friends, brother and sister, everyone's opinion of everyone else, husbands, and the end of childhood.

Later books follow Sylvia's first glimpse of modern civilisation, Arnold's future casually decided, higher education, Mrs. Marshall sticking to her principles, Sylvia skating merrily on thin ice, a bird out of a snare, and Sylvia asking herself why not. Molly, biting a sandwich, calls herself a femme watt-man, a Parisian lady motor-driver, and boasts she would die if she went under thirty-five miles an hour. Canfield's novel traces a young woman's education from Arcadian childhood to adult choice.
15244-lewie-or-the-bended-twig:
Cousin Cicely's 1854 children's book, subtitled The Bended Twig, takes its motto from training a child in the way he should go. Chapters follow little Agnes, Brook Farm, Christmas time, Cousin Betty, and a governess, through bitter disappointments, Emily's trials, and Lewie at school. A jail and a trial close the moral arc.

The book teaches that early training shapes later life, for good or ill, through stories of home, school, and temptation. Its tone is earnest, pious, and very much of the 1850s. Readers interested in early American children's fiction will find Lewie a clear sample of its moral world.
15496-the-militants-stories-of-some-pars:
Mary Raymond Shipman Andrews published this book of stories in New York in 1907, with Scribner, under the motto The sword of the Lord and of Gideon. It is dedicated to Jacob Shaw Shipman, a man who was with his whole heart a priest and with his whole strength a soldier of the Church Militant. The title names its theme: fighters, in pulpit and in camp alike.

Nine stories follow. They are The Bishop's Silence, The Witnesses, and The Diamond Brooches. Then come Crowned with Glory and Honor, A Messenger, and The Aide-de-Camp. The set closes with Through the Ivory Gate, The Wife of the Governor, and The Little Revenge. Parsons, soldiers, wives, and aides face tests of courage, love, and duty. Andrews writes warm, moral tales, where quiet endurance counts as much as battle, and faith steadies the fighter's hand.
19963-stop-look-and-dig:
George O. Smith wrote Stop, Look, and Dig, a science fiction story of hidden talents. Its narrator runs his perception up a whole city block. He takes cover behind telephone poles and front steps as he goes. By the block's end he knows it as if he had made it himself. Perception, in the story, is a sense that can be aimed and extended. Smith built many tales on such engineered abilities.

Smith was an electronics engineer who wrote for Astounding magazine. His fiction loves gadgets, signals, and competent men. A perceiving hero turns detection into a superpower of attention. The story's title twists the railroad crossing warning cleverly. Stop, look, and dig: caution becomes method. It is pulp science fiction with an engineer's soul.
20893-a-guide-to-methods-and-observation:
Historical novels like Les Miserables can teach, says Calvin Olin Davis in his guide to history teaching. Dramas, poems, essays, and reviews all earn a place in his scheme. The book, from 1914, bears the full title Studies in High School Observation in part.

Davis trains history teachers to watch classes and weigh what truly works. Methods, sources, and aims fill chapters built from real school visits. His work served the new science of teaching as schools grew vast. Readers in education can see classroom study in its earnest youth, keen to make history live for pupils, not just fill their heads.
21360-old-gold-the-cruise-of-the-jason-b:
Two wealthy Englishmen resolve to sail as far up a great South American river as anyone ever has. George Manville Fenn's tale has them choose the Amazon at last. They find the brig Jason and her skipper. Then they gain an unwelcome extra: Briscoe, a pushy young man who talks his way aboard with his stores and a servant.

It is very hot to start, in Guiana's damp, sticky heat where the muddy river looks oily. Attacks by local archers, a boat sucked toward a great cataract and saved by an eddy, and a trackway hauled past the falls follow. Above the falls they find a rock-hewn city in the cliffs, empty for centuries.
23480-what-became-of-them-and-the-concei:
G. Boare, named G. Boase at the end of the text, wrote this picture book pairing What Became of Them with The Conceited Little Pig, pictured by A. M. Lockyer. Two black rats, a he and a she, dwell in one hole and love each other well, each praising the other's long, curling, fine tail above all others.

Cheese smells, traps, and fates follow in rhyme, as the book asks what became of this pair and that, in the brisk style of nursery verse. The conceited pig of the second tale adds a second moral in miniature, on pride before a fall. Small children will enjoy the rhymes, the rats, and the pictures, which carry the jokes as much as the words, in a book designed in England and printed in Germany.
23992-a-missionary-twig:
Emma L. Burnett published A Missionary Twig with the American Tract Society in New York in 1890. Its contents trace a children's mission circle from first explanations to organized work: Edith tries to explain, Mrs. Howell tells them, and Marty gets started.

Wholes instead of tenths, the ebony chair, and the empty box teach giving in small, concrete terms. How missions helped the home folks follows, with Jennie, Laura Amelia, and the Good Shepherd. Off to the mountains, a plan and a talk, and the mountain mission-band lead to a flower sale, weeding, and hotel and garden missionary meetings. Cousin Alice's zenana work closes a earnest book of Christian service for young readers.
24731-the-tale-of-grunty-pig:
Arthur Scott Bailey wrote this animal tale in 1921 for the Slumber-Town Tales series, with pictures by Harry L. Smith. Grunty Pig is the runt of seven piglets, small but loud, and his pride and curiosity keep leading him astray. Chapters follow him through a loose board in the fence, a night locked out of the piggery, and a scare that may or may not be a bear.

The farm folk around him, from Henrietta Hen to old dog Spot, scold, guide, and rescue him in turn. Bailey writes in short, simple scenes that suit a young listener. The tale ends with Grunty wiser and back home, a gentle lesson in minding mother and not straying too far.
26029-printing-and-the-renaissance-a-pap:
John Rothwell Slater reads a paper on printing and the Renaissance before the Fortnightly Club of Rochester, printed by William Edwin Rudge in 1921 in a limited edition. Slater's thesis runs against the common view: the Renaissance produced printing, rather than printing producing the Renaissance. Libraries filled Babylon, Egypt, Greece, and Rome, and universities taught from books long before Gutenberg.

The paper traces the great publishing houses, above all the Estiennes of Paris, whose work split between sacred and secular books and typifies printing's give and take with the Renaissance. Printing reached France in 1469 through Sorbonne churchmen, five years after Italy's first press at Subiaco. Slater reminds readers that ancient and medieval thought rested on the written word, not on print alone.
28452-the-american-housewife-containing-:
The American Housewife, by an author signing herself only An Experienced Lady, reached its third edition in New York in 1841. It claims to offer the most valuable and original receipts, or recipes, in every branch of cookery. The recipes are written in a minute and methodical manner.

Beyond recipes, the book gives directions for housewifery and a collection of miscellaneous receipts. It also teaches the whole art of carving, with sixteen engravings showing how to cut beef, mutton, veal, pork, and venison. Its preface promises practical knowledge tested by good American cooks. The volume now reads as a detailed record of the early American kitchen.
29787-england-picturesque-and-descriptiv:
Joel Cook, author of A Holiday Tour in Europe, printed England, Picturesque and Descriptive, in Philadelphia in 1882. Nearly five hundred pictures fill the book, from Alton Towers in the frontispiece to an old mill at Selborne. Cook dedicates it to John Walter, member of Parliament for Berkshire and proprietor of the London Times, who welcomed Americans with true English hospitality.

Cook writes as an American for Americans. No land, he says, draws the American tourist more than England, home of his forefathers, bound to him by kin, language, laws, and customs. London streets, Liverpool docks, Devon lanes, Alnwick's walls, and the placid Wye pass in turn. The book is a rich, illustrated reminiscence of foreign travel, made to be kept and shown.
29793-the-hohokam-dig:
Theodore Pratt sets this tale at a desert dig, where two scientists take an Indian attack for a joke at first. Modern Indians did not attack white men anymore, they think, except that these attackers do. George Arthbut and Sidney Hunt, both from New York and on the staff of the Natural History Museum, lead the work. George, an ethnologist in his early sixties, studies what can be rebuilt of prehistoric Indians of the Southwest.

Sidney, an archaeologist of sixty-five, loves the ruins of the same ancient peoples. They have come west to solve the largest question left about the old cliff dwellers and desert Indians: why they left their villages. Drought, enemies, and captivity are all theories, and the Hohokam builders of Casa Grande stand at the heart of it. Pratt keeps the mystery taut and the science plain.
31-plays-of-sophocles-oedipus-the-king-o:
Three tragedies by Sophocles trace one royal house from pride to pity. The volume gathers Oedipus the King, Oedipus at Colonus, and Antigone in F. Storr's translation from the Loeb edition. Each play stands alone, yet together they follow Thebes across generations.

Oedipus hunts a killer and finds himself; blind and exiled, he later finds rest at Colonus. Antigone then defies a king's order to bury her brother. Fate, law, and family duty collide in all three. The plays remain the classic gateway to Greek tragedy. Storr's clear English keeps the choruses and debates readable for modern stage and classroom use.
3337-hunting-the-grisly-and-other-sketch:
Theodore Roosevelt writes of American big game in this volume, part two of The Wilderness Hunter. Originally published in 1893 and reprinted by Putnam in 1902, it offers an account of the big game of the United States and its chase with horse, hound, and rifle. The bison, or American buffalo, opens the chapters, with a backward look to 1776.

When the nation began, Roosevelt notes, buffaloes ranged in numbers now hard to credit. The sketches that follow track grizzly, elk, and mountain game through rough country, with rifle craft and camp life in detail. A sportsman's record that also mourns the wilderness it celebrates: Roosevelt the naturalist and hunter together.
39106-creation-myths-of-primitive-americ:
Jeremiah Curtin wrote Creation Myths of Primitive America, first tales of the land’s first folk. Little, Brown, and Company issued the book in Boston in eighteen hundred ninety eight. Curtin stands in the ruins of Palenque in its front plate. He gave the book to Major J W Powell of the Smithsonian.

Powell lost a hand in the war to save the Union, Curtin writes. That loss drove him to found the Bureau of Ethnology instead. Through that bureau the world learned the first race’s lore. Olelbis, a great sky being, heads the myths in this book. Mem Loimis stands by him in the first of the long tales. Wintu and Yana folk of California told Curtin these stores. Their sense of how the world was made fills each page. Curtin ties their thought to the whole growth of mankind.
4048-the-talkative-wig:
A children's garret tale gives voice to a wig that has seen strange doings. On a rainy Sunday, a girl sent to the garret with Pilgrim's Progress falls into a dreamy sleep, and the old things around her begin to tell their stories.

The wig recalls finding chicken and flour, and a secret kept so well that Granny Horton took its dark shape for angel wings. Willie, turning to run, let the wind lift the wig to hide him whole. Young readers will enjoy this playful fancy, where household relics speak and a small kindness becomes a marvel.
41618-chronological-retrospect-of-the-hi:
Chronological Retrospect of the History of Yarmouth and Neighbourhood, by William Finch-Crisp, is a dated list of local events. This third edition, extended and improved, runs from the year 46 to 1884. The author printed it at Great Yarmouth, with a London co-publisher.

About five thousand important local events fill the book, by its title page count. An alphabetical list of mayors adds a ready reference at the end. A quote from Locke heads the work: history owes its use and beauty to chronology. The preface notes that seven years have passed since the second edition. A proud item follows: the Prince of Wales took a copy as a gift on his visit in 1882. The author begs friends to spread the press praise and win the book a place in every library.
42153-the-making-of-a-prig:
Evelyn Sharp wrote The Making of a Prig, printed in New York and London in 1897. Sharp had written Wymps, a book of fairy tales, At the Relton Arms, and The Making of a School-Girl. The first chapter opens at supper time at the Rectory, and the Rector has not come in. The Rector disregards details; his sister prizes them. There is only one will, however, and that is his sister's.

So the meals are always on time, and the Rector is always late. This evening he is later than usual. Katharine lies on the rug like a great boy, her aunt says sharply, and bids her ring the bell for the soup. The girl rolls over lazily and shuts her book with a bang. Daddy has not come in yet, she says.
43566-a-dissertation-upon-roast-pig:
A Dissertation Upon Roast Pig is a famed light essay by Charles Lamb. Drawings by Bridgman dress this small print of the piece. A plate of Lamb heads the front of the book at its start. The book bears a rights line of the year eighteen eighty eight.

Lamb tells, from a false old scroll, how roast art was found by chance. A swine herd lad named Bo Bo plays with fire while his sire is out. The tale claims men ate raw flesh for long ages ere that day. A great sage of China is cited in jest for the raw age claim. Fond praise of crisp skin forms the true heart of the gay essay.
48264-summer-cruise-in-the-mediterranean:
Parker Willis's Summer Cruise in the Mediterranean, on board an American frigate, was issued at London in 1853 by Bosworth. The preface, dated from Highland Terrace in October 1852, calls the book the transcript of a happy episode of foreign travel. The cruise itself lay twenty years back, aboard the frigate United States as a guest of her officers. The letters keep the shape of notes written at the time.

The first letter visits Elba, Porto Ferrajo, and Napoleon's town and country houses from his confinement. Naples follows, with Herculaneum and Pompeii, then an ascent of Vesuvius and its hermitage. Later letters cover the races at Naples, the public burial ground, the museum's relics, and Paestum's Temple of Neptune. Ischia and the Bay of Naples close the early part of the cruise. The farewells were said in the port of Smyrna.
49490-an-historical-review-of-the-royal-:
An Historical Review of the Royal Marine Corps traces that corps from its first founding down to the year 1803. The work was given, with leave, to His Royal Highness the Duke of Clarence. Its price in boards was one guinea, as the title page states. The span of the book runs from the first setting up of the corps to the era of its own day.

A note by the transcriber stands at the head of the text. Old print signs for pounds have been set in a clear form for the reader. The changes of an errata list in the first print have been worked into the text. Clear slips of the pen in print have been set right by check against the rest of the book. The work is a corps history of the age of sail and of the wars with France.
58554-the-thirteen-names-of-the-first-pa:
Two sermons preached at the Obelisk Chapel on March 24 and April 3, 1811, make up this short book by the preacher Church. His text is the opening of First Chronicles, the line of names from Adam through Seth, Enosh, and Kenan down to Noah and his sons. Church reads the thirteen names of the first patriarchs as figures of the growing work of the Spirit in the soul, each name marking a stage in that progress.

The printed sermons mix doctrine with the preacher's own account of his experience, which he hoped would comfort readers who shared his faith. Published by request, the book closes with a warm letter to the woman who asked for it. It is a plain, earnest piece of chapel preaching from the first years of the nineteenth century.
59983-the-conceited-pig:
The Conceited Pig was printed in London in 1868, with six pictures by Harrison Weir. The tale opens one cold November evening. Several little pigs lie snug in their sty, keeping warm by burying their noses under the straw. One gives a loud grunt all at once, as if frightened. His mother wakes in her corner and asks angrily what the matter is.

It is only Wilful making such a noise that nobody can sleep, his brothers answer. Wilful calls for hush: he hears a great cracking the other side of the yard, and is quite sure the stables are on fire. Had they not all better go and help put it out at once? Nonsense and stuff, says his mother; he is always fancying something is the matter. She can hear no noise at all, and bids him be quiet. Wilful dares not answer, and lies still.
60205-the-cambridge-ely-and-king-s-lynn-:
Charles Harper, who wrote a shelf of books on old English roads, here takes the road from Cambridge through Ely to King's Lynn. He calls it the Great Fenland Highway. Harper drew the plates himself, as he did for the Brighton, Dover, and Bath road books.

A front plate shows the Cambridge Telegraph coach starting from the White Horse in Fetter Lane. The print is after Pollard, a famed hand at coach scenes. Harper's road books treat each highway's past and present: inns, mail coaches, and towns along the way. This volume gives the flat fen country the same care he gave the Great North Road and the mail road to Dublin.
60449-historical-record-of-the-seventy-f:
Historical Record of the Seventy-First Regiment, Highland Light Infantry belongs to an official series on the British Army. Richard Cannon of the Adjutant General's office compiled the records. They were printed by authority, under royal command and patronage. A general order of January 1836 set the whole project going. The king ordered an account of the services of every regiment. Bravery in action was to receive its full justice.

Each record had to give the regiment's formation and stations. Battles, sieges, and operations engaged in were listed. Achievements and captured colours or trophies were specified. Names of officers and counts of men killed or wounded came with place and date. The seventy first's volume follows that fixed pattern. Such records preserved a regiment's memory in official form.
60477-miss-peck-s-adventures-the-second-:
Miss Peck's Adventures is a children's tale printed at London in 1854. Joseph Masters issued it. It forms the second part of The Conceited Pig. Readers of Wilful's story, the opening says, will recall how he called Miss Peck from the henhouse one night. The two set off to tell the Queen some curious news.

They soon parted, unable to agree on the right road. Wilful's journey ended sadly, far from the palace. Miss Peck walks on alone through the dusky lane, chuckling at his folly. She means to reach the Queen's house in time, if her poor legs carry her. The tale warns its young readers through a hen's pride, as its companion warned through a pig's.
61686-so-big:
So Big is a novel by Edna Ferber of a Dutch farming district near Chicago. Grosset and Dunlap of New York issued this reprint of the nineteen twenty four book. Doubleday held the copyright, with Crowell serial rights in twenty three and four. The hero is Dirk DeJong, nicknamed So Big from babyhood on the farm.

Until near ten the name stuck, and he fought his way free of it. Sobig, the condensed form, clung in all its harsh consonant sound at school. Fists, teeth, copper toed boots, and temper won him his true name. His mother, who coined the name, stayed the worst offender in using it. The district was New Holland first, then High Prairie, southwest of Chicago.
62198-quest-of-thig:
Quest of Thig, a science fiction tale by Basil Wells, ran in Planet Stories in fall 1942. Thig of Ortha is the spearhead of a conquering horde, sent across space to subdue a defenseless world. The blurb warns that on Earth he will meet feelings more deadly than weapons. His ship lies buried on a lonely beach by the Sound, facing Connecticut.

Thig smooths sand and seaweed over the tunnel lid that joins the grubby ship to the upper air. Short, thick, and strong, with reddish brown hair and eyes, he wears only a belt for his white metal weapon and food pouches. He waits by a small highway to seize a native, intact if he can, whose mind his crew will drain.
64150-danforth-plays-the-game-stories-fo:
Danforth Plays the Game is a book of school stories by Ralph Henry Barbour, published by Appleton of New York in 1915. Its sub-title calls them stories for boys little and big. Barbour's name stood on a shelf of school sport tales: the Yardley Hall books, the Big Four, and more. The frontispiece shows Tommy hitting a ball smartly with his instep. A plate at page one hundred shows Harry romping over the line with a well-aimed pass. The first tale opens on the side line of a school field.

Four youths on the grass tease a small boy in a clean red jersey. Is the pretty little boy going to play football, they sing. Perhaps, they add, with a drawl. Danforth is the small boy, and the game is his test. Barbour writes school sport as a school of honour, in the clean series way.
70185-chateau-d-or-norah-and-kitty-craig:
Mary Holmes wrote Chateau d'Or, subtitled Norah and Kitty Craig, for Dillingham at New York. Rights were held in 1880, and the price in cloth was one dollar. A list of her popular novels fronts the book, thirty titles strong. A plate shows Haverleigh with his face buried in his hands. Contents open with Annie Strong, then the chateau itself.

Madame Verwest and Anna, and news that came to Millfield, follow in the list. News that came to the chateau, and an autumn chapter, come next. A later passage rides south in France, toward Marseilles and Nice. Hal and the teller had a train compartment to themselves all day. Holmes was praised for holding readers with deep and absorbing interest. Her pathos and sympathy made her a household name in the domestic novel.
70912-the-curse-of-yig:
The Curse of Yig is a horror tale by Reed, first set in a famed pulp sheet for weird tales in the late nineteen twenties. A note at the front tells that a long hunt found no proof its rights were made new in law. Its teller is a student of the lore of the first peoples of America.

In a set year he went into Oklahoma to hunt snake lore, he says. He came out with a dread of snakes that will last him his life. He owns the dread is a fool thing, since all he saw and heard has plain cause. His work has made him hard to tales of wild lore, red or white. What shook him was what he saw with his own eyes in a mad house in a town of that state.
9900-the-grand-old-man-or-the-life-and-p:
Richard B. Cook's biography follows William Ewart Gladstone, four times prime minister of England, from ancestry and birth through Eton and Oxford. Cook presents Gladstone as a cosmopolitan figure who stood above other premiers, active for more than half a century.

Chapters trace his early parliamentary years, his book on church and state, his travels and marriage, and his entry into the cabinet as member for Oxford. The tone is admiring, in the style of Victorian lives of great men. Readers get a full, respectful portrait of the statesman his age called the Grand Old Man.
britannica-1911-agricola-christoph-ludwi:
Christoph Ludwig Agricola (1667-1719) was a German landscape painter. He was born at Regensburg and died there. Travel filled a great part of his life. England, Holland, and France all received his visits. Naples hosted him for a considerable period too. His landscapes are chiefly cabinet pictures, small works. Fidelity to nature marks them throughout, the entry says. Varied phases of climate are his special skill. Weather and season live in his canvases.

Influences shape his manner visibly. Caspar Poussin influenced his compositions strongly. Claude Lorraine guided his light and colour. His pictures hang in many European towns. Dresden, Brunswick, and Vienna hold examples of his work. Florence and Naples hold others in Italy.
britannica-1911-ailsa-craig:
Ailsa Craig, an island rock in Scotland, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands at the mouth of the Firth of Clyde, ten miles west of Girvan in Ayrshire. Cone-shaped, with an uneven oval base, it rises sharply to 1,114 feet. Only the east side can be climbed, while the other sides are mostly sheer, with tall columnar rock forms.

Geologists prize the island's stone, a micro-granite carrying the rare mineral riebeckite, a soda amphibole. The rock type is so distinct that Professor Heddle named it ailsite. Its age is uncertain, since its links to other rocks cannot be seen on the island. Most readers, though, meet Ailsa Craig through sport. About three quarters of the world's curling-stones were estimated to be made from its granite, so curling-stones are popularly called Ailsas.
britannica-1911-almqvist-karl-jonas-ludw:
Karl Jonas Ludwig Almqvist (1793–1866) was a Swedish writer born at Stockholm. His father was a professor of theology at Upsala. Almqvist entered that university in 1808 and took his degree in 1815. Tiring of an academic career, he changed course in 1823. He led a colony of friends into the wilds of Wermland to live an ideal Scandinavian life. The experiment soon failed.

Returning to Stockholm as a teacher in 1828, Almqvist became rector of the new Elementary School. Then he turned to literature in earnest. His series of novels, The Book of the Thorn-Rose, appeared from 1832 to 1835. It made him suddenly famous. Few writers matched his output and range. Poems, romances, lectures, and treatises on philosophy, education, and religion all flowed from him. Later years brought socialist pamphlets and restless changes of post. A shadowed final chapter closes the entry.
britannica-1911-anzengruber-ludwig:
Ludwig Anzengruber, who lived from 1839 to 1889, was an Austrian playwright and novelist. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica lists his peasant dramas. He was born at Vienna in November 1839. He worked in a bookshop, then acted for seven years without great mark.

Stage time later served his writing well, the entry notes. A clerk post in the Vienna police paid his bills in 1869. Next year his play The Priest of Kirchfeld struck a hit. Its attack on priestly power made his name at once. He quit his post and lived by his pen from then on. Most plays show Austrian peasant life in a sad tone. Bright wit breaks through the gloom in scene after scene. He also wrote a praised novel and village tales.
britannica-1911-avenarius-richard-heinri:
Avenarius, Richard Heinrich Ludwig (1843-1896), was a German philosopher born in Paris and educated at Zürich, Berlin, and Leipzig, where he graduated in 1876. A year later he became professor of philosophy at Zürich, and he died there in 1896.

At Leipzig he helped found an academic philosophical society and first edited a quarterly for scientific philosophy. His chief works set out a view called Empirio-criticism, built on economy of thinking, the idea that thought should use the least force. His Kritik der reinen Erfahrung tried to explain pure experience through a person's ties to knowledge and surroundings. The entry judges his system an idealistic dualism, not realism or materialism, though he started, like Mach, from economy of thought.
britannica-1911-bamberger-ludwig:
Ludwig Bamberger (1823–1899) was a German economist and politician, born of Jewish parents at Mainz on 22 July 1823. He studied law at Giessen, Heidelberg, and Göttingen and began practice. In the revolution of 1848 he led the republican party in his home city, speaking in public and editing a local paper.

The rising of 1849 in the Palatinate and Baden brought him a death sentence, but he had fled to Switzerland. Years of exile in London, Holland, and Paris followed, where banking with Bischoffsheim and Goldschmidt taught him finance in depth. The amnesty of 1866 let him return. The 1911 Britannica entry follows his election to the Reichstag with the National Liberals and his acceptance of Bismarck's work.
britannica-1911-canitz-friedrich-rudolf-:
Friedrich von Canitz, a German court poet, is noted in a brief life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Berlin in 1654, he learned at Leiden and Leipzig. Tours of England, France, Italy, and Holland widened his young mind. Home again, he served the elector of Brandenburg at his court. He rode with that prince on his wars in Pomerania and Sweden.

In 1680 Canitz took a post as councillor of legation for Brandenburg. Missions to foreign courts filled his next years of state work. In 1697 a privy council seat and an imperial baron title came. Ill on a mission to the Hague, he won his release home. He died at Berlin in 1699, worn out by that last trip. His poems came out in print the year after his death.
britannica-1911-ettmuller-ernst-moritz-l:
Ernst Moritz Ludwig Ettmüller (1802–1877) was a German philologist born at Gersdorf near Löbau in Saxony. His father, the village pastor, taught him at home. He entered the Zittau gymnasium in 1816 and studied at Leipzig from 1823 to 1826. At Jena in 1830 he lectured on the old Norse poets. Zürich called him in 1833 to teach German language and literature at its gymnasium. He moved to the university there in 1863 and died at Zürich in April 1877.

For English studies he gave an alliterative Beowulf in 1840 and an Anglo-Saxon chrestomathy in 1850. His Lexicon Anglo-Saxonicum of 1851 explains words in Latin but orders them by root kinship. He edited many High and Low German texts. For Scandinavian letters he edited the Völuspa and translated the Nibelung lays of the Edda. His handbook of German literary history appeared in 1847. He also wrote verse tales in the old alliterative manner he admired.
britannica-1911-gieseler-johann-karl-lud:
Gieseler, Johann Karl Ludwig is a life story from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a German writer on church history. He was born on the third of March 1792 at Petershagen, near Minden, and died in 1854. His father was a preacher there. At ten he entered the orphan school at Halle.

War broke into his studies. From October 1813 to the peace of 1815 he served as a volunteer in a regiment of light horse. Back at Halle, he took his degree in 1817. He then taught at the Minden school and, in 1818, became head of the school at Cleves. There he printed his first work, a study of how the written Gospels arose. That study had strong influence on later work on the same question. In 1819 he became a professor of theology.
britannica-1911-gig: Gig is a word that seems to copy a sound, used first for any light whirling thing. Shakespeare used it for a top in one of his plays. It also named a spinning lure of feathers used to snare birds. Now it chiefly names a light two wheeled cart for one horse. It also names a narrow light boat for a ship, and a Thames rowing boat. In mining and in cloth work the word names two machines.
britannica-1911-gleim-johann-wilhelm-lud:
Johann Wilhelm Ludwig Gleim, a German poet who lived from 1719 to 1803, is profiled in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Born at Ermsleben, near Halberstadt, in April 1719, he studied law at Halle. He became secretary to Prince William of Brandenburg-Schwedt at Berlin. There he met Ewald von Kleist and became his devoted friend. When the prince fell at Prague, Gleim served another prince, but soon quit.

In 1747 Gleim was made secretary of the cathedral chapter at Halberstadt. All literary Germany called him Father Gleim for his kind patronage of poets, good and bad alike. His own verse is largely weak imitation of Anacreon and Horace. His Prussian war songs of 1758 stand higher. Inspired by the campaigns of Frederick the Second, they show genuine feeling and force. They began a long line of noble political song in German letters.
britannica-1911-hesekiel-johann-georg-lu:
Johann Georg Ludwig Hesekiel (1819–1874) was a German author, born on the 12th of August 1819 in Halle. His father, a Lutheran pastor there, was known for sacred poetry. Hesekiel studied history and philosophy at Halle, Jena and Berlin, and turned early to journalism and letters. In 1848 he settled in Berlin, where he lived until his death on the 26th of February 1874. He edited the Neue Preussische Zeitung.

He tried many kinds of work. His patriotic songs, the Preussenlieder, came out in a volume amid the unrest of 1848–1849. A second set, Neue Preussenlieder, followed the Danish War in 1864, and a third, Gegen die Franzosen, in 1870. His novels include Unter dem Eisenzahn (1864) and Der Schultheiss vom Zeyst (1875). The book he is best known by is his life of Prince Bismarck, Das Buch vom Fürsten Bismarck, which reached a third edition in 1873.
britannica-1911-michelet-karl-ludwig:
Karl Ludwig Michelet is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. He was a German thinker who lived from 1801 to 1893. He was born at Berlin in December 1801. He died in that same city in December 1893. He studied at the schools of his home town. He took his doctor grade in the year 1824. In 1829 he became a teacher and kept that post till death.

He was schooled in the doctrine of Hegel in youth. He stayed true to that teaching all his life. His work sought to guard and extend that school. A first famed work dealt with moral duty in 1828. In 1836 he brought out a French work on Aristotle. More works on Aristotle thought followed that book. His own views are best seen in two named works. Those views are called a new Christian spirit view.
britannica-1911-mond-ludwig:
Ludwig Mond is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Mond was a chemist born at Cassel in Germany in 1839. He studied at Marburg and at Heidelberg, then moved to England in 1862. He later became a British subject and built a large chemical firm.

The article tells how he found a way to recover sulphur from waste at Widnes. It then shows his part in founding Brunner, Mond and Company. The firm made alkali by a new soda process. Mond also worked on fuel gas and on a gas that joins with nickel. That find led to a clean way to take nickel from its ore. He died in London in 1909.
britannica-1911-raabe-hedwig: Hedwig Raabe (1844-1905) was a German actress, covered in a short entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in Magdeburg on 3 December 1844, she was acting at age fourteen with the Thalia theatre company in Hamburg. In 1864 she joined the German Court theatre at Saint Petersburg, touring Germany in the summers with such success that in 1868 she left to star on her own. She married the opera tenor Albert Niemann in 1871, excelled in classic roles, and was the first to play Ibsen in Berlin.
britannica-1911-straus-ludwig:
Ludwig Straus, an Austrian violinist who lived from 1835 to 1899, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Pressburg in March 1835. He studied at the Vienna Conservatorium from 1843 to 1848 as a pupil of Bohm. He first played in public in 1850 and toured Italy five years later.

In 1857 he met the cello player Piatti, his friend for life, and toured with him in Germany and Sweden. From 1860 to 1864 he led the band at Frankfort. In 1864 he made his home in England. For years he led the orchestra of Halle in Manchester and played at the Popular Concerts in London, and he was first violin in the Queen's Band. Ill health made him retire in 1893, and he lived at Cambridge till his death in 1899.
britannica-1911-wig:
Wig, short for periwig, is a false head of hair worn as an adornment, a disguise or a sign of office, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces the fashion far back. If a head covering on a prehistoric ivory carving found in a cave in the Landes is a wig, the entry says, then the fashion is some hundred thousand years old.

In historic times, wigs were worn among the Egyptians as a royal and official dress, and specimens have been taken from mummies. In Greece both men and women used them, under more than one name. A note in Xenophon on the false hair of Cyrus's grandfather, worn as was the custom among the Medes, hints that wigs came from Persia. Another tale credits immigrants into Italy from Crete as the first wearers. The frizzled hair in frescoes at Cnossus lends that idea some support.
britannica-1911-zagazig:
Zagazig, a town of Lower Egypt, is described in an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is the capital of the province of Sharkia. Its people numbered 34,999 in 1907, among them 2,617 Copts and 1,355 Greeks. The town is built on a branch of the Fresh Water canal and on an old channel of the Nile. It stands 47 miles by rail north-east of Cairo.

The article places it in the midst of rich Delta farm land. That spot made it a great centre of the cotton and grain trade of Egypt. It held large cotton factories and the offices of many merchants from Europe. About a mile south of the town lie the ruins of Bubastis, the ancient city on the same ground.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-gott:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Göttweig describes a Benedictine abbey on a hill a short way south of Krems in Lower Austria. Blessed Altmann, Bishop of Passau, founded it for Canons Regular, with the high altar dedicated in 1072 and the solemn dedication in 1083, whose charter survives in the archives.

When the canons' discipline grew lax, Bishop Ulrich of Passau, with Pope Urban the Second's permission, introduced Benedictine rule in 1094 under Prior Hartmann of St. Blasien. Hartmann brought chosen monks, founded a school, organised a library, and built a nunnery at the hill's foot, where Ava, the earliest German poetess, lived. Under Hartmann Göttweig became famed for learning and strict observance.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adam-franz-le:
Adam Franz Lennig was a theologian born at Mainz on 3 December 1803 who died there on 22 November 1866. He studied at Bouchsal under the ex-Jesuit Laurentius Doller and at the Mainz bishop's school. Not yet old enough for ordination, he went to Paris for Oriental languages under Sylvestre de Sacy. He then went to Rome for higher theology, was ordained priest on 22 September 1827, and taught a year at Mainz.

Lennig stoutly defended church rights. When the Hessian government passed thirty-nine articles on church administration on 30 January 1830, he sent them to Rome. Rome protested, but the bishops stayed silent and Bishop Burg defended the articles, so Lennig left for Bonn. In June 1832 he took the pastorate of Gaulsheim, declining a Mainz chair. In March 1848 he founded the Piusverein and organized the first Mainz meeting of Catholic societies.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-brunswick-bra:
Brunswick, a duchy in the Harz country of northern Germany, ranks tenth among the empire's states in land and people. Parcelled into three large and six small sections, it counted 464,333 people in 1900, mostly Lutherans, with 24,175 Catholics and 1,824 Jews. A constitutional monarchy of the Brunswick-Luneburg house, it lost its elder line in 1884, and Prussia barred the Cumberland heir, leaving Duke Johann Albrecht as regent.

Its town, Bruno's village, rose in the ninth century on Henry the Lion's allodial lands and passed to his grandson Otto, first duke under Frederick II. It joined the Hanseatic League in the fourteenth century. Christianity came with Charlemagne, who smashed a German idol on the site and baptized Saxons at Kissenbruck. Ludger worked near Helmstedt, and in 852 the Eastphalian duke founded Brunshausen for Benedictine nuns under his daughter Hathumod.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-bollig:
Johann Bollig, a German Orientalist born near Düren in 1821 and dead at Rome in 1895, studied theology and Semitic tongues at Rome and joined the Jesuits in 1853. In 1862 and 1863 he taught theology in Syria for native seminaries while pursuing Eastern literature.

Back at Rome, Bollig taught Arabic and Sanskrit at the Roman College and the Sapienza, served on Pius IX's Vatican Council commission as papal theologian. He consulted for Propaganda on Eastern affairs. From 1880 until death he was prefect of the Vatican Library. His printed Arabic reader and an ancient Syriac Gregory translation crown a life rich also in unpublished philology.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-konig:
Joseph König was a German theologian and Old Testament scholar at Freiburg. Born at Hausen in Baden in 1819, he was ordained in 1845 and taught at Freiburg University. His subjects were Old Testament literature and exegesis, the critical study of Scripture, from 1847 until his retirement in 1894. He died at Freiburg in 1900.

His writings include studies of immortality in Job and the theology of the Psalms, the latter judged his ablest work, plus a study of the age and origin of the Pentateuch. As editor of the Freiburg Diocesan Archive he advanced the history of Reichenau, St. Gall, and Fulda, and he wrote much on Freiburg University itself.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-leipzig:
Leipzig, chief town of Saxony at the Pleisse, Parthe, and Weisse Elster junction, held 503,672 people in 1905, of whom 22,864 were Catholics, and about 545,000 today. Its name, probably Slavonic, stays uncertain, though research proves Teutons first held the region, Slavs followed in the migrations, and Germans re-established themselves in the ninth century.

Henry I conquered the Daleminzians in 922 and fortified Meissen, and Bishop Thietmar of Merseburg first mentions Leipzig in his chronicle of 1009 to 1018. Margrave Otto of Meissen chartered it about 1160 under Magdeburg law with a major extension plan. Leipzig belonged to Merseburg diocese, its oldest church Peterskapelle yielding to the larger Nikolaikirche, and Margrave Dietrich's reign saw the Thomaskloster founded, governed by Augustinian canons, with Saxony's oldest school beside it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-schleswig:
Schleswig, once a duchy and diocese of north-west Germany, now forms part of Prussia's Schleswig-Holstein province. In the early Middle Ages southern Jutland was disputed between Germans and Danes. Its long entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows a borderland fought over by peoples, kings, and churches.

When most Germans left for Britain in the fifth century, Danes and Jutes moved in and merged with those who stayed, Frisians alone keeping their own character after losing independence. Charlemagne conquered the south about 800, made the Eider land a mark against the Slavs, and missions took root. Atrebanus, pupil of Willehad of Bremen, preached first and founded a mission station among the heathen, and the entry follows bishops and wars to modern times.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-hedwig:
Hedwig, duchess of Silesia, turned a ducal court into a workshop of charity centred on Trebnitz. Born about 1174 at Andechs castle, one of eight children of Berthold IV, she married Henry I of Silesia at twelve in 1186. Her brothers became bishops of Bamberg and Aquileia, duke of Dalmatia, and margrave of Istria, while her sister Gertrude's marriage to Andrew II of Hungary produced Elizabeth of Thuringia. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates her death at Trebnitz to 12 or 15 October 1243.

Educated at Kitzingen, she tended leper women at Neumarkt hospital with disinterested charity. At her instance Henry founded Trebnitz in 1202, Silesia's first house of religious women, endowed from his own ground and purse. Nuns from Bamberg took possession early in 1203. The entry follows a duchess whose charity built institutions, from hospital wards to a Cistercian convent that outlived her.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tewdrig: Tewdrig, or Theodoric, was a Welsh saint, son of King Ceithfalt of Morganwg. He flourished in the sixth century. He gave liberally to Llandaff church. He resigned government to his son Meurig and retired to Tintern. When Saxons under Ceolwulf crossed the Severn and pressed Meurig hard, Tewdrig left solitude, won a victory with his troops, and died in battle. A church rose over his grave, called Marthyr Tewdrig, now Mathern where Wye meets Severn. His death day was 3 January, though the year is uncertain, with 610, 577, 527, or even 470 given.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-university-of:
Leipzig's university, next to Heidelberg the oldest in the German Empire, was born from an exodus. In May 1409 German students under Johannes of Münsterberg, deposed as rector by King Wenceslaus, left Prague amid national disorders stirred by John Hus, and went to Leipzig. There Friedrich and Wilhelm, Landgraves of Thuringia and Margraves of Meissen, founded a studium generale, with a bull from Pope Alexander V at Pisa on 9 September 1409.

The charter was signed on 2 December of that year, Johannes became first rector, and 369 students matriculated in the first semester. The Bishop of Merseburg served as chancellor. At the opening of the sixteenth century Leipzig, like other German schools, felt humanism and then the Reformation. The entry follows its faculties, colleges, and scholars into the modern age, a university founded by scholars in flight.
doe-osti-2999024-multilayer-architecture:
Sumit Bhattacharya and Abdellatif Yacout of Argonne National Laboratory report in ANL/CFCT-25/24 on multilayer coatings that protect metals in hot nuclear service. Two threats drive the work. Fuel cladding can react chemically with the fuel it touches, a problem called fuel-cladding chemical interaction. Air and steam at high heat also rust zirconium alloys fast, swelling and flaking their surfaces.

The team built coatings from stacked layers of different makeup, then tested them hard. Samples faced thermal cycling, high-energy ion implantation, diffusion couple trials and strength checks. On Zircaloy-4 tubes at 800 to 900 degrees Celsius, in dry and humid air, layered coatings clearly beat plain tubes and simple one- or two-part oxide coats. Uncoated tubes grew thick oxide, spalled and swelled badly. The layered designs held their shape and slowed oxygen entry. The report judges such coatings workable for boiling water reactor conditions.
doe-osti-3022344-higher-efficiency-deman:
A final scientific report from Ultrasonic Technology Solutions, led by founder Ayyoub Momen under DOE award DE-EE0009686, covers a refrigerator project built around ultrasonic de-icing. Frost buildup forces conventional refrigerators into wasteful heating cycles. This project instead shakes frost loose with micro-vibrations on demand. The aim is a unit that is both more efficient and able to shift its load for grid demand flexibility.

The narrative runs quarter by quarter from 2021 to 2025. Partner Copeland advanced a reach-in freezer prototype through shakedown testing into experimentation. Meanwhile the team compared hybrid defrost, combining vibration with reduced heat, against thermal-only cycles. The test tracked how much melt water each method caught over time. Later milestones paired the technical demonstrations with a detailed business model and scale-up strategy for the technology.
doe-osti-3365079-a-review-of-polymeric-n:
A Review of Polymeric Nanoparticle Design, Synthesis, and Biomedical Applications, by Zoey Reese Coleman of Los Alamos National Laboratory (LA-UR-26-23904, May 2026), surveys tiny polymer carriers built to deliver medicines. The particles run from 1 to 1000 nanometers. They are made from natural biopolymers, synthetic polymers, or a mix of both. Their forms include micelles, vesicles, gels, capsules, and dendrimers.

The review shows how designers tune the polymer, size, inner structure, and surface charge. Those choices let a particle react to its surroundings and release a drug in a controlled way. Common synthesis routes include solvent evaporation, nanoprecipitation, and dialysis. Approved drugs such as Copaxone, Abraxane, and Pegasys already use the approach in patients. Newer work aims at carriers that cross the blood-brain barrier to treat brain disease.
doe-osti-3375119-kent-island-boundary-la:
Atmospheric Radiation Measurement report DOE/SC-ARM-26-021, dated June 2026, covers boundary layer soundings from Kent Island. Richard Damoah of Morgan State University led the campaign. Xiaowen Li of Morgan State and Kenneth Davis of Penn State were co-investigators. Kent Island sits on the rural side of the Baltimore study region. Its soundings fill a gap in the Coast-Urban-Rural gradient design of the CoURAGE experiment.

The team launched windsondes each week, trading day and night slots. The goal was a long, low-rate record of heat and moisture structure above the island. During the CoURAGE intensive period, launches rose to twice a day. Those extra flights left at 12Z and 18Z, timed to match soundings at the main site. A balloon system from Sparv Embedded carried the sensors.
doe-osti-3380284-next-generation-multi-u:
Next Generation Multi-Use Heavy-Duty High-Flow Direct-Fill Hydrogen Refueling Station with Standardized Design is a CRADA final report, NLR/TP-5700-99388 from July 2026, under agreement CRD-25-32768. Taichi Kuroki is the National Laboratory of the Rockies technical contact and cited author. Funding came from the Hydrogen Fuel Cell Technologies Office.

Heavy-duty hydrogen trucks need fuel fast and in large amounts, closer to a diesel stop than to a car charger. A direct-fill, high-flow station design answers that need, and the multi-use, standardized framing aims at one design that many sites can copy instead of each station being a custom build. The report closes the cooperative project and records the laboratory's part in developing the station concept.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-423sphig: GAO-05-423SPHIG of May 6, 2005, holds the short sheet of chief points from a GAO expert panel. Its theme is the Benefits and Costs of Highway and Transit Investments. The panel was not set to reach one view, but shared themes rose. Gain-cost sums can guide travel picks, the group held, if woven into the pick, not a mere check box. Modes are seldom weighed side by side. Tools to weigh land use and who gains must grow. State and town travel data must firm up.
govdocs-archive_org-the-paulician-heresy:
Nina G. Garsoian studied the Paulicians, a medieval Armenian Christian sect, in The Paulician Heresy. Her work traces the group's origin and development as a dualist movement on the eastern edge of the Byzantine world.

The Paulicians rejected much of the church's structure, its priests, and its sacraments, and the empire hunted them for it over several centuries. Garsoian works from Armenian and Greek sources to separate the sect's real teaching from its enemies' charges, which were often wild. Her study became a landmark of heresy research. The full text serves students of medieval religion who need the evidence handled with care.
hunting-the-grisly-and-other-sketches-an:
Theodore Roosevelt wrote Hunting the Grisly and Other Sketches from his years as a rancher and hunter in the American West, first published in 1893 as part of The Wilderness Hunter. Roosevelt opens with the bison, once spread across the plains in herds beyond counting. By his writing, market hunters and railroads had nearly wiped them out. He reckons fewer than five hundred wild buffalo remained.

Sketches follow the chase of big game with horse, hound, and rifle. Grizzly bears give the book its title piece. Roosevelt describes stalks, camps, and kills in close detail, along with the habits of each animal. He also mourns wasteful slaughter and praises fair chase. Readers get a hunter-president's vivid record of a vanishing frontier and the wildlife that defined it.
jack-rustig:
Frederick Marryat's tale appears here as Jack Rustig in a Dutch rendering, in a fifth printing at Amsterdam. A. J. van Dragt reworked the text, with plates by Johan Braakensiek. Nicodemus Rustig lives well at Boschlust in Hampshire in the first chapter. Childless after ten years of marriage, he turns to philosophy, the Dutch text says.

Equality and the rights of man become his hobby horse, it reports. Visitors ignore his arguments but enjoy his excellent port wine. At sea Jack wins the crew's favor, save four enemies. Vigors pales at a reminder through a cabin window. The sea tale survives in Dutch dress.
lewie-or-the-bended-twig:
Sarah H. Bradford published Lewie, or The Bended Twig, in 1854. Alden, Beardsley issued it at Auburn and Rochester, New York. A motto verse praises a mother's gentle, mighty hand.

A mother alone may train and guide her plants, the verse says. Rightly trained, they blossom sweet; neglected, they wither. Contents open with Little Agnes, then Brook Farm and Christmas time. The bended twig image promises a tale of childhood shaping. Bradford's story follows how early training bends a life. The twig proverb was a favorite of Victorian moral tales. Bradford applies it to one child's whole upbringing.
lives-of-the-english-poets-from-johnson-:
Henry Francis Cary designed these lives as Johnson's continuation. His series runs from Johnson's own era toward Kirke White. Cary also wrote The Early French Poets, published in 1846. His Pindar odes in English verse reached a second edition.

The volume extends Samuel Johnson's famous Lives of the English Poets. Later poets whom Johnson never treated receive biographies here. Cary writes as translator, clergyman, and practiced man of letters. Readers get a nineteenth-century bridge from Johnson toward the Romantics. A memoir and literary journal of Cary were preparing then. His son's generation would publish the translator's own letters later.
plays-of-sophocles-oedipus-the-king-oedi:
Sophocles' three Theban plays appear here as the Oedipus Trilogy: Oedipus the King, Oedipus at Colonus, and Antigone. The English version is by F. Storr, once a scholar of Trinity College, Cambridge. It comes from the Loeb Library edition, first published in 1912.

An argument before the first play tells the old tale in brief. An oracle warned Laius that his son would kill him and wed his mother, Jocasta. The grown Oedipus kills Laius without knowing him, solves the riddle of the Sphinx, and takes the throne and the queen. When plague strikes Thebes, his search for the killer leads to himself.
podcast-tuckercarlson-HLEA8XoxPIg:
Fighter Conor McGregor talks politics with Tucker Carlson, from his bid for Ireland's presidency to tariffs and Irish culture. McGregor, the UFC's most famous star, announced plans to run for president of Ireland. The interview mixes his campaign talk with jokes about deporting Rosie O'Donnell.

McGregor argues that Ireland's leaders are erasing Irish culture through migration and policy. He shares his views on trade and on Trump's America, which he admires. Carlson draws out the fighter's pitch to Irish voters at home and abroad. Amused and Irish viewers get the notorious star's political turn in his own swaggering words.
t-mann-der-tod-in-venedig:
An aging writer on holiday in Venice becomes obsessed with a beautiful Polish boy and stays as cholera closes over the city. Mann's Der Tod in Venedig, given here in German, is his most famous novella. Gustav von Aschenbach, disciplined master of prose, watches his lifelong self-command dissolve in the Venetian heat.

Art, desire, and decay interlock in a design of terrible perfection. Every sentence of the original German carries the music translators struggle to keep. Aschenbach's fall is stately, sordid, and pitiable at once, which is the novella's cold power. Few short books have been argued over so much for so long. It remains the essential doorway into Mann for readers worldwide.
the-bent-twig:
Dorothy Canfield published her novel in 1915 and centred it on a girl named Sylvia. Book one, called In Arcadia, opens with Sylvia's home, the Marshalls' friends, and a brother and sister. Headings promise opinions of everyone about everyone else and something about husbands.

Book two, a false start to Athens, brings Sylvia's first sight of modern life, higher education, and skating on thin ice. Some years in which nothing happens close that book. Book three, In Capua at Last, turns to talk between young moderns and brands of modern talk. Sylvia's growth from a sheltered home into a wider world shapes the whole.
the-grand-old-man-or-the-life-and-public:
Richard B. Cook wrote The Grand Old Man. Its subtitle is Or, The Life and Public Services of the Right Honorable William Ewart Gladstone. Gladstone was four times Prime Minister of England. The book opens by calling Gladstone a cosmopolitan figure. He has stood above all other premiers of the British Empire, Cook says.

For more than half a century, Gladstone was the active advocate of liberty, morality, and religion. He backed all moves for the prosperity and happiness of men. In all of it he was upright and conscientious in word and deed. He proved himself the world's champion of human rights. Cook then turns to the close of the nineteenth century. Steam and electricity have shrunk time and space. Great questions between nations now convulse the whole earth at once.
the-militants-stories-of-some-parsons-so: Mary Raymond Shipman Andrews published The Militants with Charles Scribner's Sons in May 1907, a book of stories about parsons, soldiers, and other fighters in the world. Only the title pages and dedication are present here, so the stories themselves do not appear. The title carries the motto 'The sword of the Lord and of Gideon.' Andrews dedicated the book to the memory of Jacob Shaw Shipman, described as a priest with his whole heart and a soldier of the church militant with his whole strength.
the-talkative-wig:
Mrs. Follen's Talkative Wig begins on a rainy Sunday, when a mother sends her daughter to the old garret with a copy of Pilgrim's Progress. The girl reads, grows drowsy among the queer old things stored there, and slips into a dreamy sleep. Then the garret's tenants begin to stir and speak, as they did in an earlier dream. The curling tongs, called Friend Frizzle, rises to make a complaint.

Frizzle accuses the wig of breaking a promise to tell its own life story after the other objects told theirs. The assembled things hum their approval and demand the tale. Follen turns a child's daydream into a frame for household objects recounting their histories, with the wig's long-delayed confession as the prize.
